ev.waf_h_kirina.title: The battle of Kirina
ev.waf_h_kirina.text: Sundiata Keita, son of Sogolon, has gathered the Mandinka clans against Sumaoro Kante, the dreaded king of Sosso, smith and sorcerer. The armies are converging on Kirina.
ev.waf_h_kirina.note: Around 1235 Sundiata defeated Sumaoro at Kirina and founded the Mali empire. We know of it mainly from the griots' oral epic, so the date and details are approximate.
ev.waf_h_kirina.fight.success: Sumaoro fled and Sosso fell. You came home victorious, and the griots remember your lineage's name.
ev.waf_h_kirina.fight.failure: Victory came, but you were badly wounded.
ev.waf_h_kouroukan_fouga.title: The assembly at Kouroukan Fouga
ev.waf_h_kouroukan_fouga.text: The clan chiefs have gathered on the plain of Kouroukan Fouga. Sundiata was proclaimed mansa, and the griots declared each lineage's role: who fights, who forges, who keeps the memory. They say oaths were sworn there too, to do no harm to travelers and strangers.
ev.waf_h_kouroukan_fouga.note: The tradition of the Kouroukan Fouga assembly and the "charter" that ordered Mali's society comes down through oral tradition. It was written down only in the 20th century, and historians debate how much goes back to the 13th century.
ev.waf_h_sundiata_death.title: Sundiata is gone
ev.waf_h_sundiata_death.text: News has come: Mansa Sundiata is dead. Some say he drowned in the Sankarani river, others that an arrow struck him at a festival. Griots sing laments across the land.
ev.waf_h_sundiata_death.note: The date and manner of Sundiata's death are known only from tradition; it is usually placed in the mid-1250s. He was succeeded by his son Mansa Uli, who made the pilgrimage to Mecca.
ev.waf_h_sakura.title: Sakura on the throne
ev.waf_h_sakura.text: A coup in the capital: power has been seized by Sakura, once a slave at court and no member of the Keita clan. The old nobility grumbles, but the army is his, and he is leading it on new campaigns.
ev.waf_h_sakura.note: According to Ibn Khaldun, in the late 13th century the throne of Mali was seized by a freedman named Sakura. He enlarged the empire and was killed around 1300 on his way back from the hajj. The exact dates of his reign are unknown.
ev.waf_h_sakura.grumble: Stay loyal to the Keita clan
ev.waf_h_abubakari.title: The boats sail west
ev.waf_h_abubakari.text: An incredible tale is going round: the mansa fitted out hundreds of boats to find where the great western sea ends. None came back but one. So he sailed himself with an even larger fleet, and never returned.
ev.waf_h_abubakari.note: Mansa Musa told this story in Cairo, and al-Umari recorded it. Musa's predecessor (usually called Abu Bakr II) supposedly sailed into the Atlantic. There is no corroboration, and the story remains disputed.
ev.waf_h_musa_hajj.title: Mansa Musa's hajj
ev.waf_h_musa_hajj.text: Mansa Musa is setting out for Mecca. Thousands go with him: nobles, soldiers, slaves, camels laden with sacks of gold. They say the world has never seen such a caravan.
ev.waf_h_musa_hajj.note: Musa's pilgrimage of 1324–1325 was described by Arab writers. In Cairo he gave away and spent so much gold that, according to al-Umari, its value fell for years. Mali became famous from Egypt to Europe.
ev.waf_h_musa_hajj.join.success: You saw Cairo and Mecca and came home alive, with stories for a lifetime.
ev.waf_h_musa_hajj.join.failure: The desert was cruel. You came home gravely ill.
ev.waf_h_musa_hajj.watch: See the caravan off with the whole town
ev.waf_h_musa_gao.title: The mansa in Gao
ev.waf_h_musa_gao.text: On his way back from Mecca, Mansa Musa passed through Gao. The town acknowledged Mali's rule; the mansa ordered a mosque founded and took two sons of the local ruler with him as hostages.
ev.waf_h_musa_gao.note: The Tarikh al-Sudan chronicle (17th century) says Musa visited Gao after the hajj and built a mihrab there. When exactly Gao came under Mali is disputed: it may have happened earlier, under Sakura.
ev.waf_h_djinguereber.title: The great mosque
ev.waf_h_djinguereber.text: Mansa Musa brought back from Mecca the poet and architect al-Sahili. Now a great mosque is going up in Timbuktu: the Djinguereber. Workers are paid generously, even in gold, they say.
ev.waf_h_djinguereber.note: Tradition holds that the Djinguereber mosque was built around 1327 to a design by the Andalusian poet Abu Ishaq al-Sahili, whom Musa brought back from the hajj. It has been rebuilt many times since.
ev.waf_h_djinguereber.work: Hire on at the building site
ev.waf_h_mali_timbuktu.title: Timbuktu under Mali
ev.waf_h_mali_timbuktu.text: The mansa's men have entered the town. Timbuktu is now part of the Mali empire: there is a new governor at the gate, and the merchants hope that under a strong hand the roads will be safer.
ev.waf_h_mali_timbuktu.note: Timbuktu, founded by Tuareg around 1100, became part of Mali in Musa's reign, around 1325. Under Malian rule it grew into a major center of trade and learning.
ev.waf_h_mossi_timbuktu.title: The Mossi burn the town
ev.waf_h_mossi_timbuktu.text: Mossi cavalry swept in from the south. The mansa's governor fled, and the raiders are looting houses and burning whole quarters.
ev.waf_h_mossi_timbuktu.note: The Tarikh al-Sudan reports that in Musa's time or soon after his death a Mossi king sacked Timbuktu. The exact date is unknown; the 1330s are usually suggested.
ev.waf_h_mossi_timbuktu.flee: Flee with whatever you can grab
ev.waf_h_mossi_timbuktu.hide.success: The raiders passed your house by.
ev.waf_h_mossi_timbuktu.hide.failure: They found the hiding place. You lost almost everything.
ev.waf_h_battuta_court.title: A guest from Tangier
ev.waf_h_battuta_court.text: A curious man is staying at Mansa Sulayman's court: a traveler from distant Tangier who has been, they say, to India and China. He writes everything down, and grumbles that the mansa's gift was meager.
ev.waf_h_battuta_court.note: Ibn Battuta spent about eight months in Mali's capital in 1352–1353. He praised the safety of the roads and the honesty of the people but disapproved of some court customs. Historians debate where exactly the capital then stood.
ev.waf_h_battuta_court.host: Invite the guest to your house
ev.waf_h_battuta_court.look: Have a look at the foreigner
ev.waf_h_battuta_river.title: A traveler on the river
ev.waf_h_battuta_river.text: A learned traveler from the Maghreb has arrived by boat on the Niger. He is staying with local merchants, asks about everything and tells of distant lands where people ride elephants.
ev.waf_h_battuta_river.note: Returning from Mali in 1353, Ibn Battuta traveled down the Niger through Timbuktu to Gao, which he called one of the finest cities he saw in the lands of the Sudan.
ev.waf_h_mari_djata.title: Turmoil after Sulayman
ev.waf_h_mari_djata.text: Mansa Sulayman has died, and his kinsmen are fighting over the throne. The winner, Mari Djata, rules harshly: he demands new gifts and, they say, squanders the treasury. People whisper that he even sold the ancestors' great gold nugget.
ev.waf_h_mari_djata.note: After Sulayman's death in 1360 a struggle for power began. Ibn Khaldun described the reign of Mari Djata II as cruel and wasteful, and said he sold a famous nugget from the treasury to Egyptian merchants.
ev.waf_h_mari_djata.hide.success: The collectors believed you and left.
ev.waf_h_mari_djata.hide.failure: The collectors didn't believe you and took double.
ev.waf_h_sandaki.title: Murders at the palace
ev.waf_h_sandaki.text: Blood at the palace again: one mansa killed, another overthrown, and a vizier has taken power. In the market people are afraid to say aloud whose rule it is now.
ev.waf_h_sandaki.note: Ibn Khaldun lists a series of coups in Mali in the 1380s: rulers changed quickly and power fell into the hands of viziers. The empire began to weaken.
ev.waf_h_songhai_free.title: Gao stands alone
ev.waf_h_songhai_free.text: There are no more Malian governors in Gao. The rulers of the Sonni line no longer pay tribute to the mansa and lead their own raids up the river.
ev.waf_h_songhai_free.note: When Gao broke free of Mali is not known for sure. Tradition links it to the escape of the hostages Ali Kolon and Sulayman Nar from Mali; by the early 15th century the Songhai were independent and raiding Mali themselves.
ev.waf_h_tuareg.title: The Tuareg take the town
ev.waf_h_tuareg.text: Tuareg led by Akil have entered Timbuktu. The mansa's men withdrew without a fight. The new masters roam the desert and have left their own administrator in town, and they want their share.
ev.waf_h_tuareg.note: In 1433–1434 Maghsharen Tuareg under Akil took Timbuktu, taking advantage of Mali's weakness. They left the running of the town to its local official and scholars, but levied exactions on the townspeople.
ev.waf_h_mali_north_lost.title: The north is lost
ev.waf_h_mali_north_lost.text: Bad news from the north: Timbuktu is in Tuareg hands, and the Songhai are plundering the riverbanks. Salt caravans come less often, salt grows dearer, and the mansa's men are not what they were.
ev.waf_h_mali_north_lost.note: In the 15th century Mali lost its northern possessions: Timbuktu and the Sahel towns went to the Tuareg, then to the Songhai. The empire shrank back toward its southern heartland.
ev.waf_h_portuguese.title: White men from the sea
ev.waf_h_portuguese.text: Rumors are arriving from the western provinces: huge boats with white sails have come to the mouth of the Gambia river. The strangers bring horses and cloth, and take away gold and people.
ev.waf_h_portuguese.note: From the 1440s the Portuguese sailed along the West African coast; in 1455–1456 Cadamosto went up the Gambia, where vassals of Mali ruled. The exchange of horses and cloth for captives marked the beginning of the Atlantic slave trade.
ev.waf_h_sunni_ali.title: Sunni Ali
ev.waf_h_sunni_ali.text: Gao's new ruler, Sunni Ali, is gathering cavalry and a flotilla of canoes. He prays to God but doesn't forget offerings to the ancestral spirits either. They say no one has ever seen him beaten.
ev.waf_h_sunni_ali.note: Sunni Ali (r. 1464–1492) made Songhai the greatest empire in West Africa. The Muslim chroniclers of Timbuktu portrayed him as cruel and impious; Songhai oral tradition remembers him as a great magician and warrior.
ev.waf_h_sunni_timbuktu.title: Sunni Ali takes Timbuktu
ev.waf_h_sunni_timbuktu.text: The Songhai cavalry has burst into Timbuktu. The Tuareg fled to the desert. Sunni Ali distrusts the scholars who were friendly with the Tuareg: some are executed, others flee to Walata.
ev.waf_h_sunni_timbuktu.note: In 1468 Sunni Ali captured Timbuktu. The chronicles describe persecution of scholars and the flight of many of them to Walata. Some of the exiles returned later.
ev.waf_h_sunni_timbuktu.flee: Leave with the scholars for Walata
ev.waf_h_sunni_timbuktu.lowkey: Keep your head down and wait
ev.waf_h_sunni_timbuktu.serve: Offer your services to the new ruler
ev.waf_h_djenne_siege.title: The siege of Djenne
ev.waf_h_djenne_siege.text: Sunni Ali's canoes and cavalry have surrounded Djenne. The flood protects the town, but the besiegers won't leave, and grain is running out inside. The council argues: hold out or surrender?
ev.waf_h_djenne_siege.note: Sunni Ali took Djenne around 1473. Tradition says the siege lasted seven years, seven months and seven days. The town surrendered on honorable terms, and Sunni Ali married the young ruler's mother.
ev.waf_h_djenne_siege.surrender: Side with those who want peace
ev.waf_h_mossi_raid.title: A Mossi raid
ev.waf_h_mossi_raid.text: The Mossi cavalry has swept through the district again, driving off cattle, burning villages, carrying off people. They say Sunni Ali is already marching to meet them.
ev.waf_h_mossi_raid.note: In the 1470s and 1480s the Mossi of the southern kingdoms launched long-distance raids, reaching Walata in 1480. In 1483 Sunni Ali defeated their army.
ev.waf_h_mossi_raid.defend.success: The raiders left your village untouched.
ev.waf_h_mossi_raid.defend.failure: You were wounded in the skirmish.
ev.waf_h_elmina.title: Gold flows to the sea
ev.waf_h_elmina.text: The Dyula traders are complaining: some of the gold from the forest lands now goes not north to Djenne but south to the sea. There the white strangers have built a stone fort and pay in cloth and brass.
ev.waf_h_elmina.note: In 1482 the Portuguese built the fort of São Jorge da Mina on the Gold Coast. Some of the gold that had flowed through Djenne to the Sahara turned toward the coast.
ev.waf_h_sunni_death.title: The death of Sunni Ali
ev.waf_h_sunni_death.text: Sunni Ali has died returning from a campaign. Some say he drowned at a river crossing, others that he was murdered. The throne passed to his son, Sunni Baru.
ev.waf_h_sunni_death.note: Sunni Ali died in November 1492. The chronicles say he drowned in a torrent; the circumstances of his death remain unclear.
ev.waf_h_askia.title: A new dynasty
ev.waf_h_askia.text: The general Muhammad Ture refused to accept Sunni Baru, who would not become a proper Muslim, and defeated his army at Anfao. Now he is ruler and bears the title askia.
ev.waf_h_askia.note: In April 1493 Muhammad Ture defeated Sunni Baru and founded the Askia dynasty. Askia Muhammad relied on the Muslim scholars of the towns and ruled until 1529.
ev.waf_h_askia_hajj.title: The askia's hajj
ev.waf_h_askia_hajj.text: Askia Muhammad has left for Mecca with a large retinue and hundreds of thousands of mithqals of gold. They say that in Cairo the caliph named him his deputy over all the lands of the Black peoples.
ev.waf_h_askia_hajj.note: In 1496–1497 the askia made the pilgrimage. The Abbasid caliph in Cairo recognized him as caliph (deputy) of Takrur, strengthening his authority as a Muslim ruler.
ev.waf_h_mossi_jihad.title: The campaign against the Mossi
ev.waf_h_mossi_jihad.text: The askia has declared holy war on the Mossi, who refused to accept Islam. The army is marching south, and every quarter must provide grain and men.
ev.waf_h_mossi_jihad.note: In 1497–1498 Askia Muhammad campaigned against the Mossi of Yatenga, presenting it as jihad. The army ravaged their lands but did not subdue them.
ev.waf_h_mossi_jihad.go.failure: You were badly wounded in battle.
ev.waf_h_askia_order.title: New rules
ev.waf_h_askia_order.text: The askia's decree was proclaimed in the market: the same weights and measures for all, inspectors to watch over honest trade, disputes judged by qadis according to the law. Short weight is now punished.
ev.waf_h_askia_order.note: Askia Muhammad appointed qadis to the towns, standardized weights and measures, introduced market inspection and created a standing army. His reign is seen as Songhai's golden age.
ev.waf_h_askia_order.old: Keep using the old ones until caught
ev.waf_h_askia_order.old.success: The inspector hasn't reached your row yet.
ev.waf_h_askia_order.old.failure: You were caught with the old weights. A fine and disgrace.
ev.waf_h_sankore.title: The scholars of Sankore
ev.waf_h_sankore.text: The qadi Mahmud of the Aqit family is lecturing on the law in the Sankore mosque. Students come from all over the Sahel to hear him, and books are copied day and night.
ev.waf_h_sankore.note: In the 16th century Timbuktu was one of the great centers of Islamic learning. The qadi Mahmud ibn Umar Aqit held office from 1498 to 1548; scholars taught in mosques and homes, and large libraries grew around them.
ev.waf_h_askia_deposed.title: The old askia deposed
ev.waf_h_askia_deposed.text: Askia Muhammad, old and almost blind, has been deposed by his own son Musa. The new ruler's brothers are already sharpening their knives against one another.
ev.waf_h_askia_deposed.note: In 1529 Askia Muhammad was deposed by his son Musa. Years of strife between his sons followed; the old askia died in 1538 and was buried in his tomb at Gao.
ev.waf_h_portuguese_envoy.title: An embassy from the sea
ev.waf_h_portuguese_envoy.text: Envoys of the Portuguese king have come to the mansa's court with gifts. The mansa is seeking allies against the Songhai and the Fulani, but the strangers talk mostly about trade.
ev.waf_h_portuguese_envoy.note: Around 1534 King João III of Portugal sent an embassy to Mali's ruler Mahmud II. The weakened Mali sought help against its neighbors, but no real alliance resulted.
ev.waf_h_niani_sacked.title: The Songhai in Mali's capital
ev.waf_h_niani_sacked.text: A Songhai army led by the askia's brother has burst into the capital. The mansa fled, and the foreign soldiers have spent a week in his palace dividing the spoils.
ev.waf_h_niani_sacked.note: According to the Tarikh al-Sudan, around 1545 the future Askia Dawud sacked the capital of Mali and stayed there seven days. Mali could no longer rival Songhai.
ev.waf_h_niani_sacked.hide.failure: Soldiers found your house and carried off everything of value.
ev.waf_h_dawud.title: Dawud's peaceful years
ev.waf_h_dawud.text: Under Askia Dawud the years have been peaceful. Slave villages bring in the harvests on the ruler's estates, the granaries are full, and the askia himself buys books and rewards scholars.
ev.waf_h_dawud.note: Askia Dawud ruled from 1549 to 1582. It was a prosperous time for Songhai: the ruler owned vast estates worked by slaves, patronized scholars and founded libraries.
ev.waf_h_taghaza.title: Salt grows dear
ev.waf_h_taghaza.text: Terrible news from the desert: the Moroccans have attacked the salt mines of Taghaza and killed the askia's governor. No salt caravans are coming, and the price has soared.
ev.waf_h_taghaza.note: Around 1557 the Saadian sultan of Morocco tried to seize the Taghaza mines. It was the first step toward the later invasion; salt mining eventually moved to Taoudenni.
ev.waf_h_tondibi.title: Tondibi
ev.waf_h_tondibi.text: A Moroccan army has come across the desert with firearms. At Tondibi, near Gao, the thunder of guns put the askia's cavalry to flight. The town awaits the invaders.
ev.waf_h_tondibi.note: In March 1591 the army of Judar Pasha, sent by Sultan Ahmad al-Mansur, defeated Askia Ishaq II at Tondibi. Arquebuses decided the battle, and the Songhai empire fell apart.
ev.waf_h_tondibi.fight.success: You survived the fighting, though the battle was lost.
ev.waf_h_tondibi.fight.failure: Bullet or blade, you fell and came to among the wounded.
ev.waf_h_djenne_submits.title: Moroccans in Djenne
ev.waf_h_djenne_submits.text: News has come of the askia's defeat. The elders of Djenne decided not to fight and acknowledged the pasha's rule. Foreign soldiers with guns are quartered in the town, and taxes now go to them.
ev.waf_h_djenne_submits.note: After Tondibi in 1591 Djenne submitted to the Moroccans without a long struggle. Moroccan garrisons were stationed in Timbuktu, Gao and Djenne.
ev.waf_h_scholars_exiled.title: The scholars taken away
ev.waf_h_scholars_exiled.text: The Moroccan pasha has ordered the scholars of Timbuktu seized, accusing them of sedition. Their houses were plundered, their libraries scattered, and the most famous, Ahmad Baba among them, were led in chains across the desert to Marrakesh.
ev.waf_h_scholars_exiled.note: In 1593 Pasha Mahmud ibn Zarqun arrested the scholars of Timbuktu. Many died, and Ahmad Baba and others were exiled to Marrakesh; Ahmad Baba was able to return only in 1608.
ev.waf_h_scholars_exiled.hide_books: Hide a scholar's books in your house
ev.waf_h_scholars_exiled.hide_books.succ: The chest of manuscripts stayed safely under the floor of your house.
ev.waf_h_scholars_exiled.hide_books.fail: Soldiers found the books. You were beaten and robbed.
ev.waf_h_battle_djenne.title: The mansa's last campaign
ev.waf_h_battle_djenne.text: Mansa Mahmud gathered an army to win Djenne back from the Moroccans. But beneath the town walls guns once again proved stronger than bows and spears. Mali would never regain its former glory.
ev.waf_h_battle_djenne.note: In 1599 Mali's ruler Mahmud IV tried to take Djenne but was defeated by the Moroccan garrison. Afterward the Mali empire broke up into small domains.
ev.waf_h_djenne_99.title: The town that can't be taken
ev.waf_h_djenne_99.text: The mansa's army stands before Djenne again, and again leaves empty-handed: the flood and the walls protect the town. The old people count the campaigns and say there have been nearly a hundred.
ev.waf_h_djenne_99.note: The Tarikh al-Sudan proudly says the rulers of Mali attacked Djenne 99 times and never took it. This is more local legend than an exact count; the town did at times acknowledge Mali's overlordship.
